initialContact.message: Moi! I just started vocational school and I'm living on my own for first time. I get like 650€ total from KELA (student grant + housing support) and my rent is 280€. I took out 2,500€ student loan to have some buffer. Is this enough to live on? My roommate says I should get a part-time job but I'm worried about school being hard. How do students actually manage money? I don't want to end up broke or have to move back with parents.

problemContext.currentSituation: Vocational student on his own for first time, anxious about making money last
problemContext.emotionalState: anxious, inexperienced with budgeting, wanting independence, concerned

idealAdvice: Big step living on your own - good for you!
Let's build a realistic budget for your situation:
Fixed costs: 280€ rent, 25€ utilities (shared), 30€ transport, 15€ phone = 350€
Remaining: 300€ for groceries and everything else
Left over: 100€ for other stuff (clothes, social, emergencies)
Tight? Yes. Impossible? No - many students do it!
That 2,500€ student loan is smart buffer - gives you 4-6 months breathing room
1. Student discounts: transport (50% off), restaurants (Aalto, Frank), groceries (student portions)
2. Cook at home: Lidl, S-market student prices - huge savings vs restaurants
3. Free stuff: Student union events, libraries, campus gym often included
4. Track spending first month to see where money actually goes
Part-time work question: First semester focus on adjusting to school - can add work later if needed
Electrician training has hands-on work - better to do well in school than work for 8€/hour now
Your loan buffer means you DON'T need to rush into part-time job yet
This is exactly what student loan is for - giving you space to focus on studies
Many vocational students work summers when school is lighter - good compromise
commonMistakes: Telling him 650€ is plenty without realistic budget breakdown
Pushing him to get part-time job without considering school demands
Not acknowledging the anxiety of first independent living
Not validating that having student loan buffer was smart planning
Failing to encourage him that this is achievable
